Week 1 · Day 1: Random variables and probability distributions

Goal: Understand the ideas below, reproduce a small numerical or historical example, and record a defensible conclusion. The lesson is designed for one focused 60-minute session; longer linked readings are references, not mandatory full-chapter assignments.

Subtopics explained

1. Discrete random variables and Bernoulli/binomial laws

Define a random variable as a numerical outcome of an experiment. A Bernoulli variable captures one win/loss trial; a binomial variable counts wins across a fixed number of independent trials with constant probability. In market research, trade outcomes seldom meet those independence assumptions, so explain where this simple model stops being realistic.

Textbook reading — 2nd edition (2008): §2.1 Basic Concepts (Discrete Random Variables) (printed pp. 72–73); §2.2 Probability Mass Functions (printed pp. 74–79); §6.1 Bernoulli Process (printed pp. 297–308).

2. Normal, Student-t and heavy-tailed returns

Compare a Gaussian distribution, described by mean and variance, with a Student-t distribution whose heavier tails make extreme observations less surprising. Discuss skew and kurtosis and why a good visual fit near zero does not validate a tail-risk model. Distinguish a probability density from the probability of a specific exact value.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §3.3 Normal Random Variables (printed pp. 153–157). The normal distribution is covered; Student-t fitting, heavy-tailed market returns, skewness and kurtosis require the original resource.

Study: Normal, Student-t and heavy-tailed returns (docs.scipy.org)

3. Uniform, Poisson and exponential families

Learn when the uniform law is a basic simulation benchmark, Poisson approximates independent counts in a fixed interval, and exponential models waiting times under a constant arrival rate. Contrast these assumptions with clustered trade arrivals in electronic markets. Compute one simulated example of each rather than memorizing only formulas.

Textbook reading — 2nd edition (2008): §2.2 Probability Mass Functions (printed pp. 74–79); §3.1 Continuous Random Variables and PDFs (printed pp. 140–147); §6.2 Poisson Process (printed pp. 309–323).

4. CDF, quantiles and empirical tail probability

A cumulative distribution function gives P(X ≤ x), while a quantile inverts that probability. Calculate the fifth percentile of historical returns as a descriptive loss threshold and compare it with a fitted parametric quantile. Explain why extrapolating beyond observed data is an uncertainty problem, not a plotting problem.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §3.2 Cumulative Distribution Functions (printed pp. 148–152). The CDF is covered directly; quantile estimation and empirical tail diagnostics are not a focus of these pages.

Study: CDF, quantiles and empirical tail probability (openintro.org)

60-minute study plan

  • 0–15 min: Read the first two subtopics and their source sections; write down essential equations or definitions.
  • 15–30 min: Read the remaining subtopics and one relevant linked example, focusing on assumptions and failure modes.
  • 30–55 min: Implement or analyze the targeted market experiment described below, using synthetic data when real data are unavailable.
  • 55–60 min: Save the notebook/code, a result, and an unresolved question.

Practical assignment

Simulate 10,000 returns under normal and Student-t models; plot their quantiles and count large negative moves.

Definition of done

Explain in the notebook why identical means/variances need not imply identical tail risk.

Research standard: keep the forecast cutoff explicit, separate exploratory analysis from locked evaluation, and document limitations. Study links are supplemental and may lead to longer free courses, textbooks or documentation pages.

Week 1 · Day 2: Expectation, variance, covariance and correlation

Goal: Understand the ideas below, reproduce a small numerical or historical example, and record a defensible conclusion. The lesson is designed for one focused 60-minute session; longer linked readings are references, not mandatory full-chapter assignments.

Subtopics explained

1. Expected value versus realized average

Expected value is the probability-weighted mean of possible outcomes; a sample average is an estimate from limited observations. Derive expectations for two-point outcomes and compare them with Monte Carlo estimates. Warn that an expected positive return does not establish that any particular trade or short historical window will earn money.

Textbook reading — 2nd edition (2008): §2.4 Expectation, Mean, and Variance (printed pp. 81–91); §5.2 Weak Law of Large Numbers (printed pp. 269–270).

2. Population variance, sample variance and volatility

Variance measures squared distance around the mean. Learn the distinction between dividing by n and n−1 for sample variance, and remember that standard deviation has the same units as the input. Annualizing a daily volatility by sqrt(252) assumes a particular dependence structure and trading-calendar convention.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §2.4 Expectation, Mean, and Variance (printed pp. 81–91); §9.1 Classical Parameter Estimation (printed pp. 462–476). The population moments and classical variance estimation are covered; financial volatility calculations and rolling realized estimates need the original resource.

Study: Population variance, sample variance and volatility (numpy.org)

3. Covariance and correlation matrices

Covariance describes co-movement and changes with measurement units; correlation scales to the range −1 to 1. Assemble a two-asset covariance matrix and check its eigenvalues are nonnegative. Compare correlation across rolling periods, because cross-asset relationships can move sharply during drawdowns.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §2.5 Joint PMFs of Multiple Random Variables (printed pp. 92–96); §4.2 Covariance and Correlation (printed pp. 217–221). Covariance and correlation of random variables are covered; full covariance-matrix implementation and estimation are not developed as a portfolio or numerical-algebra exercise.

Study: Covariance and correlation matrices (numpy.org)

4. Compounding and arithmetic versus logarithmic returns

Simple returns compound multiplicatively; log returns sum over consecutive periods. A sequence of +10% and −10% does not return wealth to the starting amount. Compute both mean simple returns and total compounded performance, then clarify which summary matches the research decision being made.

Study: Compounding and arithmetic versus logarithmic returns (numpy.org)

Practical assignment

Definition of done

Report estimator convention, sampling interval, and covariance units.

Week 1 · Day 3: Conditional probability, Bayes and independence

Goal: Understand the ideas below, reproduce a small numerical or historical example, and record a defensible conclusion. The lesson is designed for one focused 60-minute session; longer linked readings are references, not mandatory full-chapter assignments.

Subtopics explained

1. Conditional probability and joint events

P(A|B) describes the probability of A after restricting attention to B; it differs from P(A ∩ B). Use a contingency table for positive returns conditional on high volatility. Avoid conditioning on market information that becomes known only after the trade decision timestamp.

Textbook reading — 2nd edition (2008): §1.3 Conditional Probability (printed pp. 18–27); §2.6 Conditioning (printed pp. 97–108).

2. Bayes theorem and base-rate effects

Posterior odds combine prior odds and evidence through likelihood ratios. In a rare-event problem, even a classifier with seemingly high accuracy can generate many false alarms. Work through a toy market-crash detector with a 1% event base rate before considering its trading use.

Textbook reading — 2nd edition (2008): §1.4 Total Probability Theorem and Bayes' Rule (printed pp. 28–33); §3.6 The Continuous Bayes' Rule (printed pp. 178–181).

3. Independence versus zero correlation

Independence implies zero covariance when moments exist, but zero correlation need not imply independence. Construct X symmetric about zero and Y=X²; their relationship is deterministic despite a zero correlation. This matters when feature screens mistakenly discard nonlinear predictive structure.

Textbook reading — 2nd edition (2008): §1.5 Independence (printed pp. 34–43); §2.7 Independence of Random Variables (printed pp. 109–114); §4.2 Covariance and Correlation (printed pp. 217–221).

4. Law of large numbers and central limit theorem

The law of large numbers describes convergence of averages under assumptions; the central limit theorem concerns the distribution of suitably normalized sums. Serial dependence and heavy tails can undermine naive textbook approximations. Simulate independent samples, then compare estimates from autocorrelated samples to see the difference.

Textbook reading — 2nd edition (2008): §5.2 Weak Law of Large Numbers (printed pp. 269–270); §5.4 Central Limit Theorem (printed pp. 273–279).

Week 1 · Day 4: Confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and bootstrap

Goal: Understand the ideas below, reproduce a small numerical or historical example, and record a defensible conclusion. The lesson is designed for one focused 60-minute session; longer linked readings are references, not mandatory full-chapter assignments.

Subtopics explained

1. Null hypotheses, p-values and effect sizes

State a null such as expected net return equals zero and specify a statistic before inspecting outcomes. A p-value measures incompatibility with the null under a particular model; it is not P(null is true). Always report an economic effect size and units alongside statistical significance.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §9.3 Binary Hypothesis Testing (printed pp. 486–495); §9.4 Significance Testing (printed pp. 496–504). The book explains statistical hypotheses and significance levels; practical financial effect sizes and full testing workflow need the original source.

Study: Null hypotheses, p-values and effect sizes (docs.scipy.org)

2. Confidence intervals versus credible intervals

A frequentist confidence interval describes long-run coverage of an estimation procedure, not a probability assigned to a fixed unknown parameter after seeing data. Bayesian credible intervals rely on a posterior distribution and assumptions about priors. Distinguish both in one concise example about a strategy mean return.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §8.1 Bayesian Inference and the Posterior Distribution (printed pp. 412–419); §9.1 Classical Parameter Estimation (printed pp. 462–476). Posterior distributions and frequentist confidence intervals are addressed separately; the practical credible-interval comparison is broader than these sections.

Study: Confidence intervals versus credible intervals (ocw.mit.edu)

3. Bootstrap resampling and dependence

The ordinary bootstrap resamples independent observations; blindly resampling individual intraday returns discards serial dependence. Build an iid bootstrap as a baseline, then identify when a moving-block bootstrap or a different dependence-aware method is necessary. Assess interval stability across resampling seeds and sample lengths.

Study: Bootstrap resampling and dependence (docs.scipy.org)

4. Multiple testing and false discoveries

Searching hundreds of features inflates the chance of finding attractive noise. Compare a single-test 5% significance threshold with Bonferroni or false-discovery-rate adjustments and keep a record of tried hypotheses. Use research notebooks to make unsuccessful feature attempts visible rather than quietly removing them.

Study: Multiple testing and false discoveries (statsmodels.org)

Estimate a return mean interval by parametric and bootstrap approaches; simulate 100 null trading rules.

Definition of done

Present effect size, interval, assumptions, and a multiple-testing warning.

Week 1 · Day 5: Research lab: financial return distributions

Goal: Understand the ideas below, reproduce a small numerical or historical example, and record a defensible conclusion. The lesson is designed for one focused 60-minute session; longer linked readings are references, not mandatory full-chapter assignments.

Subtopics explained

1. Obtain and audit historical observations

Choose an accessible adjusted-close dataset and record time zone, trading calendar, corporate-action treatment, missing dates and data provider. Price returns are not volume, and a back-adjusted continuous futures series is not directly tradable. Write the data caveats before fitting any distribution.

Study: Obtain and audit historical observations (quantconnect.com)

2. Construct and inspect returns correctly

Compute simple and log returns after sorting timestamps and handling gaps. Compare daily and weekly horizons using legitimate interval aggregation. Plot summary statistics, histogram, empirical CDF and Q–Q plot; be careful not to claim independent observations simply because the sample is long.

Study: Construct and inspect returns correctly (pandas.pydata.org)

3. Fit competing distributions and inspect tails

Estimate normal and Student-t parameters on a training period and compare empirical versus model quantiles on a later period. Model fit inside a dense central region can look strong while extreme quantiles remain poor. Keep parameter estimates separate from validation data.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §3.3 Normal Random Variables (printed pp. 153–157); §4.1 Derived Distributions (printed pp. 202–216); §9.1 Classical Parameter Estimation (printed pp. 462–476). The book teaches distributional models and parameter estimation, but not Student-t tail-fitting diagnostics for financial returns.

Study: Fit competing distributions and inspect tails (docs.scipy.org)

4. Write a concise falsifiable conclusion

State which distribution fits selected diagnostics better and where evidence is insufficient. Report sample size, frequency, costs of missing observations and uncertainty in extreme quantiles. Do not convert a good in-sample histogram fit into an unsupported profitable-strategy claim.

Study: Write a concise falsifiable conclusion (matplotlib.org)

Week 2 · Day 1: Vectors, matrices and financial feature spaces

Goal: Understand the ideas below, reproduce a small numerical or historical example, and record a defensible conclusion. The lesson is designed for one focused 60-minute session; longer linked readings are references, not mandatory full-chapter assignments.

Subtopics explained

1. Vectors as observations and features

Represent each market observation as a row of measured predictors and each feature as a column. Distinguish a matrix with shape (samples, features) from a price-series vector, and establish explicit unit and timestamp conventions. A shape check is necessary but cannot detect a column assembled with future information.

Study: Vectors as observations and features (ocw.mit.edu)

2. Matrix multiplication and dot products

A linear model computes scores using a feature matrix times coefficient vector. Write out a two-feature dot product and confirm that dimensions agree before using NumPy. Explain how a vectorized implementation replaces slow Python loops without changing the mathematical operation or introducing accidental broadcasting.

Study: Matrix multiplication and dot products (numpy.org)

3. Transpose, rank and linear dependence

The transpose exchanges rows and columns. Matrix rank identifies independent directions, and collinear signals can make ordinary regression coefficients unstable. Demonstrate a design matrix containing almost duplicate moving averages and observe how fitted weights react to small perturbations.

Study: Transpose, rank and linear dependence (3blue1brown.com)

4. Scaling, norms and numerical stability

Vector norms measure magnitude while numerical conditioning indicates sensitivity to small input errors. Standardization prevents features measured in dollars and basis points from dominating optimization simply through units. Fit scaling parameters exclusively on the training segment to avoid validation leakage.

Study: Scaling, norms and numerical stability (scikit-learn.org)

Week 2 · Day 2: Eigenvectors, PCA and covariance structure

Goal: Understand the ideas below, reproduce a small numerical or historical example, and record a defensible conclusion. The lesson is designed for one focused 60-minute session; longer linked readings are references, not mandatory full-chapter assignments.

Subtopics explained

1. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors

For a square matrix, an eigenvector points along a direction that the matrix scales by its eigenvalue. For a symmetric covariance matrix, eigenvectors can be interpreted as orthogonal variance directions. Understand that numerical decomposition returns directions estimated from historical data, not guaranteed future market factors.

Study: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors (ocw.mit.edu)

2. Covariance matrices and positive semidefiniteness

A valid covariance matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite: every portfolio vector must have nonnegative computed variance. Small data samples and missing observations can produce unstable estimates. Check symmetry and eigenvalues before using a covariance estimate in portfolio optimization.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §4.2 Covariance and Correlation (printed pp. 217–221). The book defines pairwise covariance and correlation; matrix positive-semidefiniteness, eigenvalues and PCA require the linear-algebra source.

Study: Covariance matrices and positive semidefiniteness (numpy.org)

3. Principal component analysis

PCA rotates centered feature data into orthogonal directions ranked by explained sample variance. A component with high variance is not necessarily the strongest predictive trading factor. Fit PCA on training observations only, transform later observations with unchanged parameters, and compare the feature meanings before and after rotation.

Study: Principal component analysis (scikit-learn.org)

4. Factor compression versus interpretability

Reduced-dimensional factors can mitigate multicollinearity and speed computation but may obscure economically interpretable predictors. Compare two or three principal components with raw momentum/volatility features, and record the cost of lower explanatory transparency. Select the number of components using validation rather than the final holdout.

Study: Factor compression versus interpretability (statlearning.com)

Week 2 · Day 3: Derivatives, chain rule and gradients

Goal: Understand the ideas below, reproduce a small numerical or historical example, and record a defensible conclusion. The lesson is designed for one focused 60-minute session; longer linked readings are references, not mandatory full-chapter assignments.

Subtopics explained

1. Derivatives and partial derivatives

A derivative quantifies local rate of change. With multiple coefficients, partial derivatives isolate the sensitivity to each parameter while holding others fixed. In least-squares regression, connect the gradient to the direction in which predictions are systematically too high or too low.

Study: Derivatives and partial derivatives (3blue1brown.com)

2. Gradient of mean-squared error

For loss L = mean((Xw−y)²), the gradient is 2 Xᵀ(Xw−y)/n. Derive this using the chain rule and verify it with finite differences. Keep observations and feature dimensions explicit so a correct-looking formula does not conceal an unintended axis reduction.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §9.2 Linear Regression (printed pp. 477–485). The book explains least-squares regression, but does not teach gradient derivation or automatic differentiation.

Study: Gradient of mean-squared error (numpy.org)

3. Gradient descent and learning rates

Update parameters by subtracting a step proportional to the gradient. Too large a learning rate can diverge; too small a rate slows convergence and may appear stuck. Visualize the loss curve under multiple learning rates instead of assuming the optimizer succeeded because it returned a coefficient vector.

Study: Gradient descent and learning rates (docs.scipy.org)

4. Automatic differentiation versus manual gradients

Autograd builds gradients from composable operations and makes neural-network training practical. Yet it does not validate that your target is point-in-time available or that the objective matches financial utility. Compare a manual derivative with automatic differentiation on a tiny regression example.

Study: Automatic differentiation versus manual gradients (docs.pytorch.org)

Week 2 · Day 4: Convex optimization and regularization

Goal: Understand the ideas below, reproduce a small numerical or historical example, and record a defensible conclusion. The lesson is designed for one focused 60-minute session; longer linked readings are references, not mandatory full-chapter assignments.

Subtopics explained

1. Convex objectives and local versus global optima

A convex differentiable objective has no spurious local minima; a constrained convex program is often easier to reason about than arbitrary neural optimization. Recognize that an empirically convex training loss does not imply future return predictability. Solve a small least-squares problem with known optimum.

Study: Convex objectives and local versus global optima (cvxpy.org)

2. Ridge versus lasso penalties

Ridge adds an L2 penalty to shrink coefficients smoothly; lasso adds an L1 penalty that can set coefficients to zero. Both require choosing penalty strength using training/validation data. For strongly correlated financial factors, coefficient selection may be unstable even when the fitted predictions change little.

Study: Ridge versus lasso penalties (scikit-learn.org)

3. Constraints and feasible solutions

A long-only portfolio can impose weights ≥0, sum(weights)=1 and position caps; mathematical feasibility must be checked before optimizing. Add a turnover proxy or risk budget if the use case requires it. Do not use an unconstrained solution to claim execution-ready portfolio weights.

Study: Constraints and feasible solutions (cvxpy.org)

4. Out-of-sample objective choice

Minimizing training mean-squared error need not maximize net trading profit. Distinguish statistical losses from portfolio-level goals involving risk and costs. Evaluate competing objectives on the same held-out dates and report whether lower predictive error translates into a decision-relevant difference.

Study: Out-of-sample objective choice (pyportfolioopt.readthedocs.io)

Week 2 · Day 5: Research lab: NumPy optimizer from scratch

Goal: Understand the ideas below, reproduce a small numerical or historical example, and record a defensible conclusion. The lesson is designed for one focused 60-minute session; longer linked readings are references, not mandatory full-chapter assignments.

Subtopics explained

1. Prepare a nonleaking regression design matrix

Use lagged return and volatility features with the prediction target at a strictly later timestamp. Split by time before fitting normalization; treat NaNs from rolling windows explicitly. Add assertions for shape, monotonic timestamps and valid target alignment so a mathematically correct optimizer cannot quietly train on future inputs.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §9.2 Linear Regression (printed pp. 477–485). Linear regression and its assumptions are discussed, but timestamp-safe design matrices and leakage checks are outside the book.

Study: Prepare a nonleaking regression design matrix (pandas.pydata.org)

2. Implement prediction, gradient and update

Write small tested NumPy functions for loss, gradient and step updates. Validate them against finite differences on synthetic data before plugging in financial predictors. A reproducible test is more useful than a notebook screenshot that happens to show a decreasing loss on one run.

Study: Implement prediction, gradient and update (numpy.org)

3. Benchmark against standard implementations

Goal: Understand the ideas below, reproduce a small numerical or historical example, and record a defensible conclusion. The lesson is designed for one focused 60-minute session; longer linked readings are references, not mandatory full-chapter assignments.

Subtopics explained

1. Prices, returns and aggregation

Raw prices are often nonstationary and cannot be treated like iid observations. Compare simple returns, log returns and their compounding, and verify aggregation across daily versus weekly intervals. Align corporate actions or futures contract rolls before interpreting large moves as economic events.

Study: Prices, returns and aggregation (otexts.com)

2. Stationarity, deterministic trends and structural breaks

Weak stationarity requires a time-invariant mean and covariance depending on lag rather than calendar time. A visible drift or abrupt regime change can violate this picture. Examine rolling moments and discuss why a single short time series may not distinguish slow trends from structural shifts.

Study: Stationarity, deterministic trends and structural breaks (statsmodels.org)

3. Volatility clustering and heavy tails

Financial returns may show weak linear autocorrelation while absolute or squared returns show persistent dependence. This volatility clustering is an empirical feature that motivates conditional variance modeling. Check it using plots rather than assuming a Gaussian distribution with one constant variance over the entire sample.

Study: Volatility clustering and heavy tails (arch.readthedocs.io)

4. Market microstructure noise

Bid–ask bounce, discrete ticks and irregular transaction times can contaminate very short-horizon returns. Last-trade prices are not the same as synchronized midquotes, and trade-through assumptions require explicit market conventions. Identify the sampling interval at which the noise becomes important for your dataset.

Study: Market microstructure noise (arxiv.org)

Subtopics explained

1. Autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation

ACF estimates linear dependence across lags; PACF isolates a lag relationship after accounting for intervening lags in an autoregressive picture. Plot both with confidence guides but remember repeated visual inspection counts as model selection and increases false positives.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §4.2 Covariance and Correlation (printed pp. 217–221). Lagged covariance is an application of correlation; ACF/PACF for financial time series are not presented in the textbook.

2. Autoregressive baseline models

An AR(p) model predicts the next observation from past values plus an innovation. Fit simple AR models only on training data and compare to a zero-return or last-observation baseline. Financial return predictability is usually weak, so relative incremental performance matters more than a polished fit chart.

Study: Autoregressive baseline models (statsmodels.org)

3. Differencing and ARIMA

Differencing is often used to remove persistent levels before fitting ARIMA(p,d,q). Avoid differencing twice when modeling returns already derived from prices. Distinguish fitted in-sample residuals from genuine forecasts and keep an honest time-based test period.

Study: Differencing and ARIMA (otexts.com)

Subtopics explained

1. Augmented Dickey–Fuller hypotheses

ADF tests a unit-root null under specified lag and deterministic-term assumptions. A low p-value argues against that null in the tested specification; a high p-value does not prove a random walk. Run the test on prices and returns, recording the chosen regression and lag settings.

Study: Augmented Dickey–Fuller hypotheses (statsmodels.org)

2. Spurious regression and nonstationary levels

Regressing two unrelated trending price series can produce apparently strong fit and misleading significance. Demonstrate spurious regression on simulated random walks, then compare it with regression on their returns. This makes cointegration useful but also shows why naive correlations of prices are dangerous.

Study: Spurious regression and nonstationary levels (otexts.com)

3. Cointegration and error-correction intuition

Cointegration concerns a stationary linear combination of individually integrated series. A spread reverting in one sample is not automatically a stable statistical-arbitrage opportunity. Discuss hedge-ratio estimation, regime shifts and what happens when the relation breaks.

Study: Cointegration and error-correction intuition (statsmodels.org)

4. Point-in-time estimation windows

Estimate spreads, means and hedge ratios using only observations preceding the decision timestamp. Re-estimating an entire history after a test date leaks future information. Diagram how the training window advances in a walk-forward experiment.

Study: Point-in-time estimation windows (scikit-learn.org)

Under constant variance, all periods are assigned the same uncertainty; ARCH allows squared recent shocks to influence conditional variance. This can capture clustered volatility but can struggle with unexpected breaks. Inspect squared-return autocorrelation as a first diagnostic.

A simple GARCH(1,1) model combines a variance intercept, lagged squared shock and lagged conditional variance. Interpret persistence and the assumptions for a stable unconditional variance. Contrast its parametric forecasts with a basic rolling standard deviation before preferring one.

Study: GARCH recursion and persistence (arch.readthedocs.io)

A rolling standard deviation approximates past local risk, while realized variance can aggregate finer-frequency returns under data-quality assumptions. Annualize only when sampling conventions and scaling assumptions are explicit. Vary window size and show how volatility estimates lag sudden shocks.

Study: Realized volatility and rolling windows (pandas.pydata.org)

Compare predicted volatility with future realized proxy over unseen periods. Use a meaningful error statistic and inspect whether high predicted volatility corresponds to reliably higher realized volatility. The lowest training likelihood is not necessarily the most useful risk forecast.

1. Features, labels and supervised objectives

A feature vector must contain only information known by forecast time, while the label describes a later outcome. Distinguish continuous future return regression from sign classification and define the horizon explicitly. Predicting next-period sign is not the same as predicting a tradable edge after spreads and costs.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §9.2 Linear Regression (printed pp. 477–485); §9.3 Binary Hypothesis Testing (printed pp. 486–495). The book covers regression and binary hypothesis decisions, not ML feature pipelines or point-in-time trading labels.

Set a zero-return regression baseline or a majority-class classification baseline before training complex models. Examine how target class proportions vary by date and instrument. Accuracy near 50% may be meaningful or meaningless depending on class imbalance, costs and decision thresholds.

MSE penalizes large numeric errors, logistic loss grades probabilities, and neither directly encodes Sharpe ratio or execution costs. Learn the mismatch between optimizing a statistical score and optimizing a trade policy. Prefer proper predictive scoring for model development before making trading claims.

Goal: Understand the ideas below, reproduce a small numerical or historical example, and record a defensible conclusion. The lesson is designed for one focused 60-minute session; longer linked readings are references, not mandatory full-chapter assignments.

Subtopics explained

1. Linear regression predictions

Linear regression estimates a weighted combination of predictors and an intercept for a continuous response. Interpret coefficients only with attention to feature scaling and collinearity. On financial data, an apparently tiny R² can still be interesting, but only if statistically robust and economically viable.

Textbook reading — 2nd edition (2008): §9.2 Linear Regression (printed pp. 477–485).

2. Logistic regression probabilities

Logistic regression maps a linear score through a sigmoid into a class probability. A 0.55 probability forecast does not automatically imply a profitable long trade; baseline frequency, payoff asymmetry and costs matter. Examine probability calibration before using scores as risk-informed decisions.

Study: Logistic regression probabilities (scikit-learn.org)

3. L1 and L2 penalties

Use ridge/L2 to reduce coefficient magnitude and lasso/L1 to encourage sparsity. Select strength using chronological validation rather than the final test segment. Treat selected feature signs carefully because highly correlated predictors can swap estimated importance with minor sample changes.

Study: L1 and L2 penalties (scikit-learn.org)

4. Standardization inside a pipeline

Fit scalers and imputers on each training fold only, then apply to validation dates using frozen parameters. A scikit-learn Pipeline composes transformations and estimators to reduce accidental refits. Explicitly prevent global z-scores built from the entire dataset.

Study: Standardization inside a pipeline (scikit-learn.org)

A decision tree recursively divides feature space with rules such as volatility greater than a threshold. It captures interactions but can overfit noise through deep branches and repeated threshold search. Visualize a small tree before relying on hundreds of fitted splits.

Study: Decision trees and nonlinear splits (scikit-learn.org)

A forest averages noisy decision trees trained on resampled observations and feature subsets. Standard iid bootstrap assumptions differ from time-series dependence, so chronological testing is still essential. Compare forest predictions with a simpler linear baseline on identical target rows.

Boosting builds a sequence of trees correcting the current model’s errors. Learn learning rate, maximum depth, subsampling and early stopping; tune only inside the training/validation range. A large boosted model can memorize market regimes without useful forward performance.

Study: Gradient boosting and XGBoost (xgboost.readthedocs.io)

Subtopics explained

1. Confusion matrix, precision and recall

A confusion matrix separates true and false signals by direction. Precision measures correctness among predicted positives, while recall measures coverage of actual positives. For trading, a high false-positive rate may consume spread costs, but a high recall can also be economically weak without payoff information.

2. ROC AUC, PR AUC and Brier score

ROC AUC evaluates ranking across thresholds, precision–recall metrics emphasize positive-event retrieval, and Brier score evaluates squared probabilistic errors. Compare models using metrics matching the hypothesis and class balance. Do not choose whichever metric happens to give the most flattering result.

A calibrated 0.6 probability prediction should correspond to roughly 60% positives across comparable repeated cases. Use reliability bins and Brier/log loss on held-out dates. Small bins in changing markets are unstable, so show counts and uncertainty instead of claiming perfect calibration.

A quoted spread is best ask minus best bid; a midprice averages the two. Midquote returns avoid some last-trade bounce, but a midquote is generally not an executable trade price. Use bid for an immediate sale and ask for an immediate purchase when modeling crossing costs.

For level-1 bid quantity B and ask quantity A, imbalance can be (B−A)/(B+A) when the denominator is positive. Larger imbalance can indicate short-term pressure but is sensitive to order cancellation, stale updates and exchange rules. Preserve event ordering when deriving it.

Study: Depth and order-book imbalance (arxiv.org)

4. Microprice and order-flow changes

A common microprice weights quotes using opposite-side size and may lead the midprice under some conditions. Contrast the static level imbalance with changes in quoted depth and order-flow imbalance. Avoid presenting any of these features as universal predictors across markets or holding horizons.

Week 5 · Day 3: Lagged features, rolling windows and leakage

Goal: Understand the ideas below, reproduce a small numerical or historical example, and record a defensible conclusion. The lesson is designed for one focused 60-minute session; longer linked readings are references, not mandatory full-chapter assignments.

Subtopics explained

1. Lagging predictors to prediction time

For a forecast made before the close, a same-day closing price is not yet available. For a forecast after the close, it may be available but the execution opportunity differs. Create an explicit forecast timestamp and shift features accordingly; an off-by-one shift often creates a spectacular but false backtest.

Study: Lagging predictors to prediction time (pandas.pydata.org)

2. Rolling windows and warm-up periods

Moving averages, exponential moving averages and rolling quantiles require lookback data and a declared minimum number of observations. Drop or flag warm-up rows instead of filling them with future-aware estimates. Unit-test the earliest valid index and values from a short hand-computable series.

Study: Rolling windows and warm-up periods (pandas.pydata.org)

3. Cross-sectional ranks and normalization

Ranking momentum within an asset universe can remove scale and emphasize relative opportunities. The universe must be knowable at the past decision date; filtering today’s surviving tickers backward creates survivorship bias. Normalize cross-sectional features using the contemporaneous eligible universe only.

Study: Cross-sectional ranks and normalization (quantconnect.com)

4. As-of joins and delayed information

Joining economic, news or fundamental data by observation date can falsely assume instant publication. Use as-of joins based on actual availability timestamps, include processing lags and audit late revisions. If a reliable publication timestamp is unavailable, use conservative delays and label the estimate uncertain.

Study: As-of joins and delayed information (pandas.pydata.org)

Subtopics explained

1. Univariate relationships and information coefficient

An information coefficient measures association between predicted scores and future returns, often via rank correlation. Compute it separately by date or group and aggregate rather than conflating all overlapping observations with independent evidence. Explain how IC differs from actual portfolio profit.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §4.2 Covariance and Correlation (printed pp. 217–221). Correlation of random variables is covered, but financial information coefficients and cross-sectional factor evaluation are not.

2. Correlation matrices and redundant predictors

A large list of related technical indicators may encode only one underlying effect. Use pairwise correlations and optionally hierarchical clustering or PCA to identify groups. Removing redundant features is not always necessary for tree models, but it makes ablation and interpretation easier.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §4.2 Covariance and Correlation (printed pp. 217–221). Pairwise correlation is covered; redundant multivariate predictors and matrix diagnostics require the original ML resource.

3. Permutation importance and holdout discipline

Permutation importance estimates the change in a trained model’s score after disturbing one feature. Correlated predictors can conceal one another’s importance, and random shuffling may create unrealistic temporal patterns. Evaluate on validation dates and interpret alongside economic rationale.

Study: Permutation importance and holdout discipline (scikit-learn.org)

Split feature performance by volatility regime, asset and calendar subperiod using predeclared bins. A strong average can be driven by one crisis month, so report dispersion and counts. Do not tune regime definitions using the final test set merely to rescue a weak result.

1. Why random K-fold is unsafe by default

Random folds mix early and late observations and can leak regime information or overlapping labels into training. With financial prediction, the validation procedure must simulate when a model would actually have been estimated. Compare random versus chronological scores on a nonstationary simulated series.

Study: Why random K-fold is unsafe by default (scikit-learn.org)

Use training for fitting, validation for choices such as feature sets or hyperparameters, and a locked test period for the final claim. Record period boundaries and rationale before tuning. Repeated looks at the final test convert it into a hidden validation set.

Study: Train/validation/test separation (scikit-learn.org)

3. Expanding versus rolling windows

An expanding window accumulates observations and can reduce variance, while a rolling window discards older data and may adapt faster to market changes. Compare them with identical forecast horizons and costs; neither universally dominates when the data-generating process shifts.

Study: Expanding versus rolling windows (scikit-learn.org)

4. Forecast origin and information sets

Every prediction should carry forecast origin, feature cutoff and label interval. A prediction on Friday’s close differs from one placed before that close. Use explicit time metadata to guarantee that each fold’s model sees only records available before its decisions.

A five-day forward-return label at t and another at t+1 share most of their price path. Treating their scores as independent exaggerates effective sample size. Represent the start and end of every outcome interval before building folds.

Remove training rows whose label information intervals overlap the validation/test label interval. Distinguish dropping by event-time overlap from naively removing a fixed number of rows. Check boundary cases using synthetic labels with precisely known start and end times.

An embargo blocks a period around a fold boundary where information contamination or serial dependence is plausible. Purging is not a cure for survivorship bias, publication-timing errors or feature choices discovered on the test set. Combine interval-safe splitting with honest universe definitions, point-in-time joins and a research log. Inspect original timestamps rather than trusting a library helper blindly.

Goal: Understand the ideas below, reproduce a small numerical or historical example, and record a defensible conclusion. The lesson is designed for one focused 60-minute session; longer linked readings are references, not mandatory full-chapter assignments.

Subtopics explained

1. Look-ahead bias in features and targets

Look-ahead occurs whenever future data influence inputs or decisions. Centered rolling averages, global standardization and future-adjusted corporate actions may introduce subtle examples. Write a test where changing data after time t cannot change any predictor computed for t.

Study: Look-ahead bias in features and targets (scikit-learn.org)

2. Survivorship and universe selection

Selecting stocks that exist today and replaying them in the past excludes failed or delisted names. This can materially distort a cross-sectional model even when train/test dates are perfect. Record the available historical universe and acknowledge when the dataset cannot fully eliminate survivorship bias.

Study: Survivorship and universe selection (quantconnect.com)

3. Hyperparameter search and winner’s curse

Searching many thresholds or models on a noisy validation period makes the winning score optimistic. Restrict the search space using theory, preserve a locked holdout and report the number of attempted configurations. A small chosen model can be more defensible than a heavily optimized one.

Study: Hyperparameter search and winner’s curse (statlearning.com)

4. Feature fit boundaries and future revisions

Dataset revisions, forward-filled later fundamentals and transforms estimated on all dates can leak information. Audit preprocessing at the level of each fold, not just at the final estimator. For macroeconomic series, distinguish reference periods from release timestamps.

Week 7 · Day 3: Portfolio variance, diversification and risk budgeting

Goal: Understand the ideas below, reproduce a small numerical or historical example, and record a defensible conclusion. The lesson is designed for one focused 60-minute session; longer linked readings are references, not mandatory full-chapter assignments.

Subtopics explained

1. Portfolio expected return and risk

Portfolio expected return is wᵀμ and variance is wᵀΣw for weights w, estimated means μ and covariance Σ. Interpret the uncertainty of both inputs. Estimated mean returns are particularly noisy, so optimal portfolios can be unstable without shrinkage or practical constraints.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §2.4 Expectation, Mean, and Variance (printed pp. 81–91); §4.2 Covariance and Correlation (printed pp. 217–221). Linearity of expectation and covariance are mathematical ingredients of portfolio variance, not a complete portfolio-risk model.

Study: Portfolio expected return and risk (pyportfolioopt.readthedocs.io)

2. Diversification versus correlation

Diversification changes risk through cross-asset covariance, not simply by increasing the count of holdings. Compare two positively correlated assets with a lower-correlation pair. Correlations can change under stress, so historical diversification is conditional evidence rather than a guarantee.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §4.2 Covariance and Correlation (printed pp. 217–221). The covariance/correlation identity explains why co-movements matter; portfolio diversification analysis is not taught directly.

Study: Diversification versus correlation (numpy.org)

3. Risk contribution and volatility targeting

Portfolio variance and marginal risk contributions connect position sizes to aggregate uncertainty. A volatility target scales exposure down when estimated risk rises, but the estimate may lag shock events and induce turnover. Distinguish ex-ante risk budgets from ex-post realized contributions.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §4.2 Covariance and Correlation (printed pp. 217–221). Covariance supports variance calculations, but marginal risk contribution and volatility targeting need the portfolio source.

Study: Risk contribution and volatility targeting (pyportfolioopt.readthedocs.io)

4. Mean–variance optimization caveats

Efficient-frontier calculations can amplify noise in expected returns and covariance estimates. Compare equal-weight, inverse-volatility and constrained mean–variance weights before preferring the most sophisticated optimizer. Include concentration and turnover as explicit practical concerns.

Study: Mean–variance optimization caveats (cvxpy.org)

A portfolio update incurs turnover proportional to the change from current to target weights. Penalizing turnover or using no-trade bands can reduce cost but may delay response to signals. Tune cost assumptions from plausible market conditions, not the final test’s most favorable outcome.

Sample covariance matrices can become unstable when assets are numerous relative to observations. Shrinkage moves estimates toward a structured target and can improve conditioning. Study: Shrinkage and robust covariance estimation (scikit-learn.org)

Position caps, concentration limits and volatility budgets are design constraints rather than guarantees against loss. Drawdown rules may realize losses after a shock and can increase turnover. Calculate covariance and volatility from a trailing window ending before rebalancing. Apply shrinkage or diagonal simplifications as explicit model choices. Never feed realized future returns into an optimizer while retrospectively scoring its decisions.

Subtopics explained

1. Query, key and value vectors

Attention compares a query to keys and uses the resulting weights to aggregate value vectors. Work through a tiny dot-product attention calculation with a small sequence. Attention weights are learned computation, not an automatic or causal explanation of why a financial event affected market prices.

Study: Query, key and value vectors (jalammar.github.io)

2. Scaled dot-product attention and softmax

Dot products measure similarity but grow in magnitude with vector dimension; scaling by the square root of key size keeps softmax behavior more manageable. Explain masking and numerical normalization. Compare attention with recurrence, including computation cost for long documents or long market sequences.

Study: Scaled dot-product attention and softmax (docs.pytorch.org)

3. Position information and sequence order

Without positional information, a basic attention block alone lacks a direct representation of word or time order. Positional embeddings or encodings provide sequence placement. In finance, token order is meaningful, but the actual public release timestamp is also essential and must be stored outside the text representation.

Study: Position information and sequence order (jalammar.github.io)

4. Encoder representations versus generative LLMs

Encoder-style models can produce contextual representations and classification scores; autoregressive models generate text token by token. Select the simpler architecture suited to the research question. A fluent model explanation cannot substitute for a timestamp-aligned quantitative validation of its output.

Study: Encoder representations versus generative LLMs (huggingface.co)

Current web pages and cleaned company histories may revise or remove items that were different at historical decision times. Re-running today’s model on historical text is an ex-post experiment unless historical availability is modeled.

Study: Survivorship and historical document revisions (sec.gov)

If a language model summarizes or labels documents, fix prompts and model versions and examine output stability and hallucinations. Keep labeled examples separate from downstream test events, and never let the model browse future price outcomes while creating a historical feature.

Week 10 · Day 1: Markov decision processes and rewards

Goal: Understand the ideas below, reproduce a small numerical or historical example, and record a defensible conclusion. The lesson is designed for one focused 60-minute session; longer linked readings are references, not mandatory full-chapter assignments.

Subtopics explained

1. States, actions, transitions and episodes

An MDP represents a process by states, actions, next-state transitions and rewards. For trading, states might include lagged features and current inventory, while actions are hold, buy or sell. Historical replay is not truly Markov when hidden liquidity and market impact are unobserved.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §7.1 Discrete-Time Markov Chains (printed pp. 340–345). The book develops Markov states and transition probabilities; MDP actions, rewards and episodes require the reinforcement-learning resource.

Study: States, actions, transitions and episodes (incompleteideas.net)

2. Reward design and transaction costs

Gross mark-to-market PnL rewards encourage overtrading unless spreads, commissions and inventory risk are penalized. Define rewards as changes in portfolio value after costs with a consistent execution timestamp. A reward calculated using the next price before choosing the action is a critical look-ahead bug.

Study: Reward design and transaction costs (spinningup.openai.com)

3. Discount factor and trading horizon

The discount factor controls how future rewards influence current policy optimization. Relate it to episode length and economic holding period, but do not interpret it literally as a market interest rate. Compare a myopic versus longer-horizon planning preference on a simple deterministic toy environment.

Study: Discount factor and trading horizon (incompleteideas.net)

4. Observability, stationarity and distribution shift

Trading agents often see an incomplete market state, and transitions can shift during crises or rule changes. A strategy optimized on one historical episode may exploit replay quirks that fail in live markets. Define environment limitations before choosing a powerful learning algorithm.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §7.3 Steady-State Behavior (printed pp. 352–361). Steady-state behavior of Markov chains is covered; POMDP observability and real-market distribution shift are not.

Study: Observability, stationarity and distribution shift (gymnasium.farama.org)

Subtopics explained

1. State value versus action value

V(s) estimates expected discounted reward from a state, while Q(s,a) evaluates choosing a particular action first. In a simple tabular market toy problem, work out Q values from finite transitions. Do not treat estimated Q values as directly calibrated profit forecasts.

Study: State value versus action value (incompleteideas.net)

2. Bellman recursion

The Bellman equation decomposes a value into immediate reward plus discounted expected future value. Derive a two-step example and distinguish evaluation of a fixed policy from maximizing across candidate actions. This recursive relation motivates dynamic programming and temporal-difference learning.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §7.1 Discrete-Time Markov Chains (printed pp. 340–345); §7.4 Absorption Probabilities and Expected Time to Absorption (printed pp. 362–368). Markov transition and first-step recursions are useful prerequisites; Bellman optimality with actions and rewards is not developed here.

Study: Bellman recursion (spinningup.openai.com)

3. Temporal-difference updates and exploration

Q-learning updates action values using observed rewards and a bootstrap estimate of later value. Explore-versus-exploit decisions are feasible in a simulator but have real market cost and risk. Limit the experiment to historical/synthetic data rather than suggesting online exploration with live capital.

Study: Temporal-difference updates and exploration (incompleteideas.net)

4. Deep Q networks and function approximation

DQN uses a neural network to approximate Q values for discrete actions, typically with replay and target-network stabilization. Such techniques address training instability but do not solve market nonstationarity. Prefer a tabular baseline in a tiny toy environment before increasing complexity.

Study: Deep Q networks and function approximation (stable-baselines3.readthedocs.io)

1. Observation and action spaces

Define gymnasium spaces that make shapes, value ranges and valid actions explicit. Observations should use lagged features and current portfolio state; if hidden future returns slip into the observation, training will reward cheating rather than genuine prediction.

reset initializes episode state; step executes an action and returns the next observation, reward, termination/truncation flags and diagnostic info. Follow the API carefully so episode endings do not accidentally give agents a free liquidation outcome or look-ahead signal.

Study: Inventory, cash and mark-to-market accounting (quantconnect.com)

Train agent parameters on historical training intervals, select hyperparameters on validation episodes and reserve later test episodes. Normalize observations using development data only. Reusing the same fixed trajectory repeatedly can generate an overfitted memorization policy even if the Gym API is correct.

1. Formulating a falsifiable financial hypothesis

A research claim should specify population, information set, horizon, expected effect and evaluation metric before examining the final data. “AI finds alpha” is not falsifiable; “lagged volume improves 1-day Brier score beyond momentum by a predefined margin” is testable.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §9.4 Significance Testing (printed pp. 496–504). Formal statistical hypotheses and significance tests are explained; writing a falsifiable financial research protocol needs broader methodology.

Study: Primary, secondary and exploratory analyses (nber.org)

3. Strong and weak benchmark design

A sophisticated model should be compared with constant forecasts, historical average, linear baselines and simple economic rules where appropriate. An intentionally weak baseline inflates perceived progress. Match data availability, constraints and costs across comparators.

Study: Strong and weak benchmark design (statlearning.com)

4. Effect size and practical significance

A statistically detectable AUC improvement may be too small to survive execution costs. Express improvements in interpretable units: basis points of net return, Brier reduction or reduction in risk. State the minimum practically meaningful effect before looking at the final result.

Week 11 · Day 2: Bootstrap confidence intervals for dependent data

Goal: Understand the ideas below, reproduce a small numerical or historical example, and record a defensible conclusion. The lesson is designed for one focused 60-minute session; longer linked readings are references, not mandatory full-chapter assignments.

Subtopics explained

1. Why iid confidence intervals can mislead

Consecutive financial returns can be autocorrelated or volatility-clustered, and overlapping forward labels share outcomes. Treating each row as an independent draw artificially narrows uncertainty estimates. Inspect temporal dependence before choosing a resampling method.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §1.5 Independence (printed pp. 34–43); §5.4 Central Limit Theorem (printed pp. 273–279); §9.1 Classical Parameter Estimation (printed pp. 462–476). Independence and the CLT underlie classical intervals; the book does not teach dependence-robust inference or block bootstrap.

Study: Why iid confidence intervals can mislead (statsmodels.org)

2. Moving-block bootstrap intuition

A block bootstrap resamples consecutive chunks instead of isolated observations, retaining some short-range dependence within each chunk. Select block length as a sensitivity parameter rather than the value that produces the strongest significance. Discuss limitations for long memory and changing regimes.

Study: Moving-block bootstrap intuition (docs.scipy.org)

3. Intervals for paired model differences

When two models predict the same timestamps, resample paired differences or paired paths to preserve their shared outcomes. Do not bootstrap models separately and mistake the resulting independent samples for a comparison. Report the interval for the incremental metric, not only separate model intervals.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §9.1 Classical Parameter Estimation (printed pp. 462–476). Classical confidence intervals are covered; paired dependent bootstrap intervals for model differences are not.

Study: Intervals for paired model differences (docs.scipy.org)

4. Confidence interval interpretation and sample size

A confidence interval has coverage only under assumptions about the data-generating process and resampling scheme. Short financial histories and rare events leave large uncertainty even after thousands of bootstrap replicates. Report effective sample limitations and sensitivity to block size.

Textbook reading — 2nd edition (2008): §5.4 Central Limit Theorem (printed pp. 273–279); §9.1 Classical Parameter Estimation (printed pp. 462–476).

Week 11 · Day 3: Multiple comparisons and realistic significance

Goal: Understand the ideas below, reproduce a small numerical or historical example, and record a defensible conclusion. The lesson is designed for one focused 60-minute session; longer linked readings are references, not mandatory full-chapter assignments.

Subtopics explained

1. Why factor discovery creates false positives

If many candidate signals are tested against the same noisy returns, impressive winners occur by chance. Track the full search count including abandoned experiments. Treat a result discovered through massive tuning as exploratory unless validated on a new, untouched dataset.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §9.4 Significance Testing (printed pp. 496–504). The meaning of a false statistical rejection is covered; multiple exploratory factor tests require correction methods not in the book.

Study: Why factor discovery creates false positives (nber.org)

2. Family-wise error and Bonferroni correction

Bonferroni limits family-wise false-positive risk by dividing the significance level across tests, though it can be conservative under dependence. Apply it to a toy set of p-values and explain its tradeoff versus the raw 0.05 cutoff.

Textbook foundation — 2nd edition (2008), partial coverage: §1.2 Probabilistic Models (printed pp. 6–17); §9.4 Significance Testing (printed pp. 496–504). The probability union bound (see p. 14) and basic significance tests provide a foundation; the book does not teach Bonferroni-adjusted family-wise error control.

Study: Family-wise error and Bonferroni correction (statsmodels.org)

3. False discovery rate with Benjamini–Hochberg

FDR control manages the expected fraction of false discoveries among selected rejections under conditions on test dependence. Compare FDR to family-wise error control when examining a group of related candidate features. Do not interpret q-values as exact probabilities that individual hypotheses are false.

Study: False discovery rate with Benjamini–Hochberg (statsmodels.org)

4. Selection bias and out-of-sample replication

Statistical corrections do not completely repair an adaptive research workflow that repeatedly consults final test outcomes. Reserve a later replication interval or different instrument universe, and distinguish replication from yet another search on the same evidence.

Study: Selection bias and out-of-sample replication (nber.org)

Compute wealth-compounded net returns, annualized volatility where assumptions permit, maximum drawdown, Sharpe ratio and turnover. Also examine number of trades and regime concentration. A good classification score can coexist with poor profit after costs.

Study: Measure return, drawdown, turnover and exposure (github.com)

Change at least two defensible factors such as cost, training-window length, prediction threshold or data subperiod without retuning on test. Interpret any collapse in performance as fragility. State whether the result is statistically supported, economically meaningful, both or neither.
